response.evidence: These figures come from a manual count of the rows and are approximate. Hispanic or Latino male applicants were approved most of the time: about 20 denials out of roughly 150 applications, an approval rate of about 87%. Their raw denial rate (about 13%) is higher than for White males (about 8%) and Asian males (about 6%). However, most of those denials match standard risk factors rather than ethnicity alone. About half had debt-to-income ratios of 50% or more, and many others had very low incomes (for example $46k–$74k) or loan-to-value ratios of 95–100%+. In contrast, several Hispanic males with high debt-to-income ratios were approved (for example 50%-60% at $475k, $625k, $655k and $755k, and >60% at $1.085M and $1.015M), which argues against systematic bias. White and Asian males with similar risk profiles were also denied. A few Hispanic male denials have moderate profiles (for example 30%-<36% debt-to-income with $243k income and 75% loan-to-value, or 20%-<30% with $225k income), but White males show similar unexplained denials. Hispanic male applicants in this sample also tend to have lower incomes and higher loan-to-value ratios than White and Asian applicants, which may explain the raw gap. This data cannot rule out discrimination, since it omits credit scores and other factors lenders use, but it does not show clear evidence of it.
